en: The Diamond Cutter Sūtra on the Perfection of Wisdom Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Yijing of the Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Bhagavān was staying in the city of Yaśovatī, in the Saṃgrāmajaya Forest.
Having given the Jetavana Grove as a gift, he was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as a multitude of great bodhisattvas.
At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
Having completed his alms round in sequence, he returned to his original location.
When he had finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and sat cross-legged upon the seat previously prepared, dwelling in right mindfulness.
At that time, the bhikṣus approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to sit on one side.

Then, the Venerable Subhūti, amidst the great assembly, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How rare! How marvelous!”
World-Honored One!
How rare!
Well-Gone One!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is able to benefit all bodhisattvas with the most supreme benefit;
he is able to entrust all bodhisattvas with the most supreme entrustment.
"Bhagavān!
If there are those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle, how should they dwell?
How should they practice?"
"How does one subdue and control the mind?
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"So it is, so it is! It is as you have said:
'The Tathāgata benefits all bodhisattvas with supreme benefit;'"
"Because it is entrusted with excellence, I entrust it to all bodhisattvas. "O Subhūti!
You should listen attentively and apply your mind most skillfully; I shall analyze and explain it for you."
“Those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle should abide in this way, practice in this way, and thus subdue their minds.
Subhūti said, “So be it, World-Honored One!”
"I wish to hear it with joy.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"If there are those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle, they should give rise to this thought:"

"Of all classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the worlds, such as these, I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation."
"Although he has thus caused immeasurable sentient beings to realize parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has entered parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Wondrous Birth!..."
If a bodhisattva has the notion of a sentient being, they are not called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because they possess the notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life-span, and the notion of one who seeks further rebirth.
"Furthermore, Subhūti,
a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling upon things;
they should practice giving without dwelling upon any location."
One should practice giving without dwelling on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles,
or mental phenomena. Subhūti,
when a bodhisattva gives in this manner, they should not dwell even on the perception of signs.
Why is this? Because by not dwelling upon giving, the accumulation of merit is difficult to measure. "O Subhūti!
"What do you think?
Is it possible to measure the extent of space in the eastern direction?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! " [The Buddha asked:
"In the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, above and below—in the ten directions throughout empty space—can its measure be known?
Maitreya said:
"No, World-Honored One. "Excellent Birth!
It is likewise with the mass of merit obtained by a bodhisattva who practices giving without abiding."
“Wondrous Birth!
What do you think?
Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of the possession of excellent marks?”
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One!
One should not view the Tathāgata by means of marks of excellence."
Why is this? That which the Tathāgata calls the "excellent mark" is, in fact, not an excellent mark. "O Subhūti!
All superior marks are false and illusory.
If there were no superior marks, they would not be false and illusory.
Therefore, one should contemplate the Tathāgata through the marklessness of superior marks.
Subhūti said: “World-Honored One,

will there be any sentient beings in the future age, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is about to perish, who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, will give rise to true faith?”
The Buddha told Wonderful Birth:
"Do not speak thus:

'Will there be any sentient beings in the future age, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, will give rise to true faith?'"

“Subhūti! In future ages, there will be bodhisattvas who are endowed with precepts, virtue, and wisdom. These bodhisattvas have not merely served and made offerings to a single Buddha to plant roots of goodness;
they have already served and made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, planting roots of goodness.”
Such a person is indeed able to give rise to even a single thought of faith in this sutra. "Subhūti!
The Tathāgata fully knows such a person; the Tathāgata fully sees such a person. Those bodhisattvas shall produce and gather an immeasurable mass of merit."
Why is this? Because those bodhisattvas have no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of one who seeks further rebirth.
Those bodhisattvas have no notion of phenomena, no notion of non-phenomena, no notion, and no non-notion.

Why is this? If that bodhisattva has the notion of a phenomenon (dharma-saṃjñā), they possess the grasping at a self (ātma-grāha), the grasping at a sentient being (sattva-grāha), the grasping at a life-span (jīva-grāha), and the grasping at a person who seeks rebirth (pudgala-grāha).
If one has the notion of non-dharma, they likewise possess the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-span, and the grasping at a seeker of rebirth.
Subhūti, for this reason, a bodhisattva should neither grasp at dharma nor grasp at non-dharma.
For this reason, the Tathāgata has intentionally proclaimed the Dharma-door of the raft parable: "O wise ones, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not Dharma."
“Wondrous Birth!
What do you think?
Has the Tathāgata realized anything in regard to unsurpassed enlightenment?”
"Furthermore, is there even the slightest dharma that has been taught? Subhūti replied,
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the Tathāgata has in truth realized nothing in unsurpassed enlightenment, nor has he taught anything."
Why is this? The Dharma taught by the Buddha cannot be grasped and cannot be expressed; it is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Why is this?
"Because all noble ones are manifested by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"If a good son or a good daughter were to take seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift, would they gain much merit?
Subhūti replied,
"Very much, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? This accumulation of merit is not an accumulation; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as an accumulation of merit, an accumulation of merit. “O Subhūti!
If there are sons or daughters of good family who take the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm and offer them as a gift;

and if there is another person who, regarding this sutra, can even take up and uphold a single four-line verse, or explain it for others—by reason of these causes and conditions, the mass of merit produced will be far greater than that, immeasurable and incalculable.
Why is this? Wondrous Birth!
It is because the unexcelled perfect enlightenment of all Tathāgatas emerges from this sutra.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are born from this sutra.
Therefore, Subhūti!
What the Tathāgata calls the Buddha-dharma is not Buddha-dharma; it is merely designated as "Buddha-dharma."
“Wondrous Birth!
What do you think?
Do those who have entered the stream ever harbor such a thought:”
"Did you think, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this?
Those who are stream-enterers have no dharma into which they enter; therefore, they are called 'stream-enterers.'"
Because they do not enter into form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental phenomena, they are called "stream-enterers.
World-Honored One,
if a stream-enterer were to have this thought:

"One who says, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry,' possesses the grasping at a self, the grasping at a sentient being, the grasping at a life-span, and the grasping at one who seeks further rebirth. Subhūti! "
What do you think?
Do those who are once-returners ever have this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of once-returning"?
"Is this not so? Subhūti replied,
"It is not so, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest dharma by which one realizes the state of a Once-returner; therefore, he is called a "Once-returner.
"Wondrous Birth! [It is so.]”
What do you think?
Do those who are non-returners ever have this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of non-returning"?
"Is this not so? Subhūti replied,
"It is not so, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? Because there is not even the slightest dharma by which one realizes the state of a non-returner; therefore, one is called a "non-returner.
"O Wondrous Birth!..."
What do you think?
Do any Arhats ever have this thought:
"I have attained the fruit of Arhatship"?
"Is this not so? Subhūti replied,
"It is not so, World-Honored One!"
Because there is not even the slightest dharma that can be called an "Arhat," O Bhagavan!
If an Arhat were to have such a thought:

"World-Honored One, one who says, 'I have attained the fruit of Arhatship,' possesses the grasping at a self, as well as the grasping at a sentient being, a life-span, and a seeker of further rebirth."
"The Tathāgata has declared that I am the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇāvihārin*).
World-Honored One!
Although I am an Arhat free from the defilement of desire, I have never actually entertained such a thought:"
"World-Honored One! If one were to think: 'I am an Arhat.'"
Regarding those who say, "I have attained arhatship," the Tathāgata does not say that I, Subhūti, am the foremost among those who dwell in the state of non-contention (*araṇā-vihāra*).

Because there is absolutely nothing upon which to dwell, it is said that I have attained the dwelling in non-contention; it is for this reason that it is said I have attained the dwelling in non-contention.
“Subhūti! What do you think?
When the Tathāgata was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, was there even the slightest dharma that could be grasped?”
Subhūti said: “Not so, World-Honored One!
Under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, there was truly nothing for the Tathāgata to take up.”
“Wondrous Birth!
If there is a bodhisattva who speaks thus:
‘I shall accomplish the adornment of a buddha-field,’ [he does not speak the truth].”
To say this would be a false speech. Why?
That which is called "adorned buddha-fields" the Tathāgata has said is not adorned; it is for this reason that it is called the adornment of a field.
Therefore, Wondrous Birth!

A bodhisattva should not abide in things, should not abide in locations, and should not abide in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena; they should generate a mind that does not abide in these.
They should generate a mind that does not abide in things, a mind that does not abide in locations, and a mind that does not abide in forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena.
“Wondrous Birth!
Suppose there were a person whose body was as large as Sumeru, the King of Mountains.
What do you think? Would that body be great?”
Subhūti said:
“It is very great, World-Honored One! Why is this so?”
"That which is called a 'great body' by the Tathāgata is, in fact, not a body.
Because it does not exist as such, it is designated as a 'body.
" "Wondrous Birth! "
What do you think?
If there were as many Gaṅgā rivers as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, would the grains of sand in all those rivers be numerous?
Subhūti said:
"Very many, World-Honored One!
The rivers themselves are already innumerable, how much more so their sands."
“Subhūti! I now tell you the truth.
If there were someone who, with treasures filling as many worlds as there are grains of sand in this river, were to offer them to the Tathāgata, would they gain much merit?”
Subhūti said,
“Very many, World-Honored One! “Subhūti!

If, moreover, there should be someone who receives and upholds even a single verse from this sutra and explains it to others, this mass of merit would surpass the previous mass of merit by an immeasurable and boundless degree.

“Subhūti! If there is this Dharma-gate in any land, and it is explained to others, even if only as a single four-line verse, you should know that this spot is a caitya; all devas, humans, and asuras should circumambulate it to the right and pay homage to it.
How much more so for one who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety—you should know that such a person is the most supreme and the foremost among the rare.”
Furthermore, this very place shall have a Buddha and his honored disciples.
"Subhūti, what do you think?"
“Is there even the slightest dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata?
Subhūti replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"There is not even the slightest dharma that has been taught by the Tathāgata.
"Wondrous Birth!
As for all the particles of dust in the earth of this trichiliocosm, would these be many?"
Subhūti said:
“Very many, World-Honored One! Why is this?”
"What the Buddha calls 'dust of the earth' is not dust; therefore it is called 'dust of the earth.
These so-called 'worlds' are not worlds; therefore they are called 'worlds. "O Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the thirty-two marks of a great man?
Subhūti replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is this? Because..."
“The thirty-two marks, the Buddha says, are not marks; therefore they are called the marks of a Great Man.
“Wondrous Birth!
If there were men or women who, with as many lifetimes as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, gave them away in alms;”

"If there were another person who, from within this sutra, were to receive and uphold even a single verse and explain it to others, their merit would surpass that [previous merit] by an immeasurable and incalculable amount.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this teaching of the sutra, deeply understood its meaning and intent; with tears flowing and weeping sorrowfully, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"
“World-Honored One!
Since the arising of my wisdom, I have never before heard such a profound sutra as this,
World-Honored One!”
"What should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?
The Buddha told Miaosheng:
"This sutra is named 'Prajñāpāramitā'; it should be upheld in this way. Why is that?
What the Buddha calls 'Prajñāpāramitā' is not, in fact, Prajñāpāramitā."
“World-Honored One!
If there should be another person who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, gives rise to the thought of its reality, you should know that such a person is most supreme and rare.
World-Honored One!”
This perception of reality is itself not a perception of reality; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it as the "perception of reality," the "perception of reality.
World-Honored One, that upon hearing this sutra my mind gave rise to faith and understanding is not particularly rare.
If, in a future age, there should be those who hear this sutra and are able to receive and uphold it, such persons would be the most rare and wonderful.
Why is this? Because those people will have no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of a seeker of rebirth.
Why is this so? World-Honored One!
The notion of a self, the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a life span, and the notion of one who seeks rebirth—these are, in truth, not notions.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are free from all conceptualizations.
"O Wondrous Birth! "
"So it is, so it is! If there should be anyone who, upon hearing this sutra, is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear, you should know that such a person is the most rare of all."
Why is this so? O Subhūti!
This most excellent pāramitā is the pāramitā taught by the Tathāgata among all pāramitās.
That which the Tathāgata speaks was proclaimed by boundless Buddhas; therefore, it is called the supreme pāramitā. "Subhūti!
What the Tathāgata calls the kṣānti-pāramitā is not, in fact, a kṣānti-pāramitā."

Why is this? When I was formerly having my limbs and body cut apart by the King of Kalinga, I had no notion of a self, no notion of a sentient being, no notion of a life-span, and no notion of seeking further rebirth.
I have neither this perception nor the absence of perception. Why is this?
If I were to possess this perception, I would give rise to resentment and hatred.
"O Wondrous Birth!
Furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi practicing patience; at those times, I had no such perceptions as these.

Therefore, you should abandon all perceptions and set out toward the mind of unsurpassed bodhi; you should not dwell on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas, but rather give rise to that mind by dwelling nowhere at all."
One should not dwell on dharmas, nor should one dwell on non-dharmas; thus should the mind be generated.
Why is this? If there is anything upon which one dwells, that itself constitutes non-dwelling.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything.
"Wondrous Birth! (Subhūti!)"
A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner.
This notion of "sentient beings" is itself not a notion;
those so-called sentient beings are, in reality, not sentient beings.
Why is this? Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from all conceptualizations,
O Wondrous Birth!
The Tathāgata is one who speaks truth, one who speaks as it is, one who does not speak deceptively, and one who does not speak otherwise. "O Subhūti!
The Dharma realized by the Tathāgata and the Dharma taught by him—this is neither real nor false."
“Wondrous Birth!
If a bodhisattva dwells upon phenomena while practicing giving, it is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all.

If one practices giving without dwelling upon phenomena, it is like a person with eyes, when the sun shines brightly, seeing all manner of forms. Therefore, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling upon phenomena.”
“Wondrous Birth!

If there are good men or good women who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain this sutra for others, such persons as these are fully known and fully seen by the Buddha with his eye of wisdom; they shall produce and gather immeasurable masses of merit.”
“Wondrous Birth!

If there were good sons or good daughters who, during the first part of the day, gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the middle part of the day, again gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; and during the latter part of the day, likewise gave away as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—continuing in this manner for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas, giving away their bodies as an act of charity.”

If there should be another person who, upon hearing this sutra, does not give rise to slander, their merit would surpass that [of the former]; how much more so for one who copies it, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, and explains it to others.
“Wondrous Birth!

This sutra possesses inconceivable, immeasurable, and boundless merit; it is taught by the Tathāgata for those who have set out upon the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out upon the Supreme Vehicle.”

If there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite [this sutra], and extensively explain it to others, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all; they shall all achieve an accumulation of meritorious karma that is immeasurable, incomparable, and inconceivable. You should know that such persons are carrying the unexcelled Bodhi of the Tathāgata upon their shoulders.
Why is this? Subhūti!

Those who delight in inferior dharmas are attached to the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of seeking further rebirth. It is impossible for such persons to read, recite, accept, and uphold this sutra.
“Wondrous Birth!

Wherever this sutra may be found, you should know that such a place is a caitya; it is worthy of being revered, saluted, and circumambulated by all the world—including devas, humans, and asuras—and one should offer various fragrant flowers to that location.”
“Wondrous Birth!
If there are good men or good women who, at the time of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and expounding this sutra, are perhaps slighted or insulted by others.”
Why is this? Wondrous Birth!

You should know that such a person, having created various evil karmas in previous lives, was destined to fall into the evil realms; because they now encounter slight humiliation, this becomes a virtuous matter, for it enables them to exhaust their evil karma and swiftly reach Bodhi.
“Wondrous Birth!

I recall that in the past, more than incalculable eons ago, before the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I encountered eighty-four billion nayutas of Buddhas; I made offerings to and served them all, never acting in opposition to any of them.”

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, during the final five hundred years when the True Dharma is perishing, is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, understand its meaning and intent, and explain it extensively for others—the merit they obtain cannot be matched by the former merit even at one hundredth part; nor can it be reached by a thousand-million-billionth part, nor by calculation, nor by estimation, nor by comparison, nor by number, nor by cause, nor even by analogy.
“Wondrous Birth!
If I were to fully describe the merit of upholding, reciting, and reading this sutra, some who hear it would have their minds become deranged, falling into doubt and lack of faith.”
“O Subhūti!
You should know that this sutra is inconceivable; those who receive and uphold it should expect an inconceivable accumulation of merit to arise.”
"Furthermore, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
'World-Honored One!
If there are those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle.'"
"How should one dwell?
How should one practice?
How should one subdue and control the mind?"
The Buddha told Wonderful Birth:
"If there are those who have set out upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, they should give rise to this thought:
'I shall deliver all sentient beings, causing them all to enter nirvana without remainder.'"
"Although there are thus immeasurable sentient beings who have realized parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has realized parinirvāṇa. Why is this?
Wondrous Birth!
If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a "sentient being," they cannot be called a bodhisattva.
Why is this? O Wondrous Birth!
"In reality, there is no dharma that can be called one who has set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
"At the place of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, was there even the slightest dharma that was realized?
Subhūti replied,
"At the place of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there was no dharma to be realized by which he attained bodhi."
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is, Subhūti!"
In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata realized at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara by which he attained great bodhi.
If there were a dharma to be realized, then the Buddha Dīpaṃkara would not have conferred upon me this prediction: "O Māṇava!..."
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
Because there was nothing to be attained, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction that I would attain Buddhahood, with the name Śākyamuni.
Why is this? Wondrous Birth!
That which is called "Tathāgata" is simply another name for the true nature of suchness.
“Wondrous Birth!
If one were to say:
‘The Tathāgata has realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.’”
To say this would be a falsehood.
Why? Because, in reality, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has realized as unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
"O Subhūti!
The Dharma of perfect enlightenment attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal.
Therefore, the Buddha says:"
"All dharmas are indeed the Buddha-dharmas. Subhūti!
As for "all dharmas, all dharmas," the Tathāgata says they are not dharmas; therefore, what the Tathāgata calls "all dharmas" are indeed the Buddha-dharmas.
“Subhūti! It is as if there were a man whose body was tall and large. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata calls ‘one of great body’ is, in fact, said to be no-body; it is merely named ‘great body.
The Buddha told Miaosheng:
"So it is, so it is! If a bodhisattva should say:
'I shall deliver sentient beings and bring them to nirvana.'"
“...then they would not be called bodhisattvas. Subhūti!
Is there even the slightest dharma that can be called a 'bodhisattva'?”
He replied, “No,
World-Honored One. “Excellent Birth!
Therefore, the Tathāgata has said:
"All dharmas are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without a person who seeks further rebirth.
"O Wondrous Birth! [Listen well!]"
If there is a bodhisattva who says,
"I shall accomplish the magnificent adornment of a buddha-field,
the magnificent adornment of a buddha-field," the Tathāgata says that it is not a magnificent adornment; therefore, the Tathāgata calls it a magnificent adornment.
"O Subhūti!

If there are those who have faith and understanding that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature, and that all dharmas are without intrinsic nature, the Tathāgata declares them to be truly Bodhisattvas, Bodhisattvas."
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?”
Subhūti said: “So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the divine eye.”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye.”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.”
“Subhūti! What do you think?
Suppose there were as many Gaṅgā Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Gaṅgā River, and for each grain of sand in those rivers, there were as many worlds; would these be numerous?”
Subhūti said,
“Very many, World-Honored One! “Subhūti!
"O Miao-sheng! I fully understand all the various dispositions and conducts of the sentient beings in this world, as well as the wandering of their minds.
Why is this? O Miao-sheng!"
As for the dhāraṇī of the mind, the Tathāgata says it is "without grasping. Because it is without grasping, the mind consequently flows on.
Why is this so, O Wondrous Birth?
"The past mind cannot be apprehended; the future mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended.
Subhūti, what do you think?"
“If a person were to give as an offering the seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm, would that person gain much merit?
Subhūti replied,
“Very much, World-Honored One!”
“O Subhūti! If this accumulation of merit were truly an accumulation of merit, the Tathāgata would not have called it an ‘accumulation of merit’ or a ‘pile of merit. O Subhūti!”
"What do you think?
Can the Tathāgata be perceived by means of the perfection of the physical body?
"No, World-Honored One."
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*). Why is this?
That which is called the "perfection of the form-body," the Tathāgata has said, is not a perfection; it is for this reason that it is called the "perfection of the form-body."
“Subhūti! Can one perceive the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks?
“No, World-Honored One!”
One should not perceive the Tathāgata by means of the marks of physical perfection. Why is this?
That which the Tathāgata calls the marks of physical perfection, the Tathāgata says is not the marks of physical perfection; therefore, it is called the marks of physical perfection.
“Subhūti! What do you think? Does the Tathāgata have such a thought as this:”
"Do you think, 'I preach the Dharma'?
Do not hold such a view.
If one says,
"The Tathāgata has preached any Dharma," then that person slanders me.
"Why is this? As for 'the teaching of the Dharma' and 'one who teaches the Dharma,' there is no dharma that can be taught; it is merely called 'teaching the Dharma.
Subhūti said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this sutra being preached, will give rise to faith?
The Buddha told Miaosheng:
“Those who give rise to faith are neither sentient beings nor non-sentient beings. Why is this?
What are called ‘sentient beings’ have been taught by the Tathāgata to be non-sentient beings; they are merely designated as ‘sentient beings.’”
“Subhūti, what do you think? When the Buddha attained unsurpassed,
perfect, and complete awakening, was there even the slightest dharma that was realized?”
Subhūti said: "In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that has been realized by the Buddha.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"So it is, so it is! Within this, not even the slightest dharma can be apprehended; therefore, it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti! "
This Dharma is equal, without high or low; therefore it is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Because it is without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, and without a nature that seeks further rebirth—its nature being equal—it is therefore called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because all wholesome dharmas are perfectly awakened to, it is called "Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment.
Subhūti! What are called wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata has declared them to be non-dharmas; therefore they are called wholesome dharmas.
“Wondrous Birth!
If there were someone who, using as a gift all the heaps of the seven treasures equal in measure to all the Sumeru Kings within a trichiliocosm, were to bestow them in charity;”

Furthermore, if there should be someone who, from this sutra, even takes up and maintains a single four-line verse, whether for themselves or for others, then compared to that mass of merit, let it be divided into a hundred parts;

even one part of those [previous merits] could not equal it. Nor could a thousandth part, a hundred-millionth part, a calculated part, a proportional part, a numerical part, a causal part, or even a metaphorical illustration equal even one part of it.
“Wondrous Birth!
What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata deliver sentient beings?”
Do not hold such a view as this:
"The Tathāgata delivers sentient beings. Why is that?
There has never been a single sentient being who was delivered by the Tathāgata.

If there were any sentient beings delivered by the Tathāgata, then the Tathāgata would possess the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of one who seeks further rebirth.
“Wondrous Birth!
What we call ‘grasping’ the Tathāgata has declared to be non-grasping; yet foolish commoners falsely conceive of it as grasping.
Wondrous Birth!”
“Ordinary beings, the Tathāgata says, are not beings; therefore they are called ‘ordinary beings.
Wondrous Birth!
What do you think?”
"Should one view the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks?
"No, World-Honored One!
One should not view the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks."

“Subhūti! If one were to view the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks, then a Wheel-Turning Sage King would also be a Tathāgata. Therefore, one should not view the Tathāgata by means of his physical marks; rather, one should view the Tathāgata by means of the non-existence of all marks.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If one sees me by means of form, Or seeks me through sound,
Such a person gives rise to false contemplation And shall not be able to see me.”
One should contemplate the nature of the Buddha-dharma; it is the Dharma-body of the Teacher.
Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) cannot be known through cognition, it cannot be fully understood by them.
"O Wondrous Birth!..."
"Is the dharma of those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle something that is subject to annihilation?
Do not hold such a view. Why is this?
Those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle do not lose their dharma. "Subhūti!
If there were a man or a woman who were to give as an offering the seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā."

Furthermore, if there should be another person who attains patient acceptance and understanding regarding the principle of non-self and the non-arising of phenomena, the mass of merit produced by that person would be infinitely and incalculably greater than the former.
“Wondrous Birth!
A bodhisattva should not grasp at that mass of merit.
Wondrous Birth said:
“Does a bodhisattva not take up a mass of merit?
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“He should take it correctly; he should not take it erroneously. For this reason, it is said that he takes it.”
“Wondrous Birth!
It is as if someone were to say:
‘The Tathāgata comes or goes, sits or lies down.’”
"Those who say this do not understand the meaning of what I have taught.
Why is that? O Wondrous Birth! "
Because there is absolutely no coming or going, he is named Tathāgata.
“O Wondrous Birth!
Suppose there were a man or a woman who ground the earth of a trichiliocosm into fine dust.”
"Subhūti, what do you think?
Is this accumulation of atoms indeed much?"
Subhūti said:
"Very much, World-Honored One! Why is this?"
If the nature of an aggregate were real, the Tathāgata would not have spoken of it as "an aggregate of atoms, an aggregate of atoms.
Why is this? That which is called an "aggregate of atoms" was described by the Blessed One as not being an aggregate of atoms; it is for this reason that it is called an "aggregate of atoms."
World-Honored One!
That which the Tathāgata calls the "trichiliocosm" is said to be a non-world; therefore, it is named the "trichiliocosm. Why is this?
If the world were substantially existent, the Tathāgata would possess a grasping at aggregates.
What the Buddha calls "grasping at aggregates" is said to be non-grasping at aggregates; therefore, it is called "grasping at aggregates."
“O Wondrous Birth!
This grasping at an aggregate is a worldly convention; however, its essential nature is truly ineffable, being merely a false attachment of foolish ordinary beings.”
“Wondrous Birth!
It is as it has been said:
‘The Buddha spoke of the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, and the view of one seeking further rebirth.’”
"Is this a correct teaching or an incorrect one?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One!"
Why is this? If there is such a thing as a "view of self" spoken of by the Tathāgata, it is actually not a view;
therefore, it is called the "view of self. "O Subhūti!
All those who have set out upon the bodhisattva vehicle should, regarding all phenomena, know them thus, see them thus, and understand them thus.
One who understands them thus does not dwell even in the notion of "phenomena."
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is called "the notion of phenomena" (dharmasaṃjñā), the Tathāgata has taught it to be a non-notion; therefore it is called "the notion of phenomena."
“Wondrous Birth!
If there were someone who took seven treasures filling immeasurable and incalculable worlds and offered them as a gift;

and if there were another person who, regarding this sutra, could even receive, uphold, read, and recite a single four-line verse, mastering it thoroughly and correctly explaining its meaning to others—by reason of these causes and conditions, the mass of merit produced would be far greater than that immeasurable and incalculable amount.”
"What is correct teaching?
That there is no dharma that can be taught—this is called correct teaching.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are like stars, a visual impairment, a lamp, a magical illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, and a cloud; one should contemplate them in this way."

At that time, when the Bhagavān had finished speaking this sutra, the Venerable Subhūti, along with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and all those in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and others—all rejoiced greatly, and having faith and acceptance, they practiced accordingly.
The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Which Can Sever [All Attachments]
